hints: Look closely at the line X-Y across the mitochondrion and measure it yourself with a ruler in millimetres. What length do you get on paper?
Remember magnification = image size divided by actual size, so first convert the actual length of 3000 nm into the same units (mm) as your measurement.
walkthrough:
**Measure the image size**

Grab a ruler and measure the line X-Y on the drawing. You should get about 30 mm.

This is your image size:
$$image = 30 \text{ mm}$$

**Convert the actual size to the same units**

The actual length is given as 3000 nm. We need this in mm to match our ruler measurement.

Remember: $1 \text{ mm} = 1,000,000 \text{ nm}$, so:
$$actual = 3000 \text{ nm} = 0.003 \text{ mm}$$

**Apply the magnification formula**

Magnification is simply how many times bigger the image is than the real thing.

$$magnification = \frac{image \text{ size}}{actual \text{ size}} = \frac{30}{0.003} = 10,000$$

So the drawing is x10 000, which is option C. Well done!

options.A: Too small. x100 would make a 3000 nm mitochondrion only 0.3 mm long on paper, much smaller than the drawing.
options.B: Still too small. x1000 would give an image of only 3 mm, about ten times shorter than the X-Y line you measure.
options.C: Correct. A 30 mm image divided by a 0.003 mm actual length gives x10 000 magnification.
options.D: Too large. x100 000 would give an image of 300 mm (30 cm), far bigger than the drawing shown.
